grid_reliability.name: Grid Reliability & Resiliency
grid_reliability.content: The power supply in South Korea, managed by KEPCO, is one of the most reliable in the OECD, with continuous efforts toward system improvement and modernization, including the deployment of a Distribution Automation System (DAS) to reduce outages significantly. Grid stability is high, though it faces increasing complexity due to the planned integration of variable renewable energy (VRE) generation.
key_points: World-class grid reliability metrics (SAIDI < 10 min/year).
High grid stability, critical for hyperscale operations.
KEPCO has strong disaster recovery and continuous system maintenance programs.

power_capacity.name: Power Capacity & Scalability
power_capacity.content: The Greater Seoul Metropolitan Area (Gyeonggi-do) is heavily congested, with data center power demand requests projected to significantly outpace available supply capacity (7,343 MW requested by 2027 vs. 4,718 MW supply capacity). However, KEPCO is investing 72.8 trillion KRW (~$53.9 billion) through 2038 to increase transmission capacity and add nearly 400 substations, including 'electric highway' HVDC lines to the metropolitan area, which will eventually support 100MW+ scalability.
key_points: Significant capacity strain in the metropolitan area requires extensive lead time.
Massive KEPCO investment addresses long-term capacity and transmission needs.
Scaling to 100MW+ is feasible but dependent on KEPCO's 11th Long-Term Plan project timelines (2024-2038).

generation_mix.name: Power Generation Mix & Sustainability
generation_mix.content: South Korea's power mix relies heavily on fossil fuels (approx. 55-60%), with coal and gas making up a large portion. Nuclear energy (around 30-32%) provides a stable, low-carbon baseload. Renewable energy (non-nuclear) penetration is relatively low (approx. 6%), resulting in a moderate grid carbon intensity (~380 gCO2/kWh). The new energy plan prioritizes nuclear and 'carbon-free' sources to reach a 70% carbon-free mix by 2038.
key_points: Moderate carbon intensity poses a challenge for strict net-zero goals.
Strong nuclear baseload provides stability and a low-carbon option.
Low VRE penetration requires creative Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) solutions.

connection_process.name: Connection Process & Regulatory Framework
connection_process.content: The grid interconnection process for large-scale projects, overseen by KEPCO and MOTIE, has become significantly more stringent and time-consuming in the Greater Seoul area. Confirmation of power supply now takes up to 12 months (up from 2-3 months), and the overall process for a 50MW+ connection is estimated at 18-36 months, driven by grid congestion and new energy efficiency regulations for data centers. The government favors decentralization to regional areas.
key_points: Extended power confirmation timeline (up to 12 months) in the metropolitan area.
Stringent new energy efficiency regulations for permitting.
Need to closely coordinate with KEPCO and MOTIE due to decentralization policy.

electricity_costs.name: Electricity Costs & Market Dynamics
electricity_costs.content: Industrial electricity rates for high-voltage, large-scale users rose to approximately KRW 182.7/kWh (~$0.135/kWh) in October 2024, a significant surge of over 70% since 2022. This rate is higher than those in major US/China data center hubs, reducing competitiveness. Pricing is volatile and subject to politically-charged hikes aimed at reducing KEPCO's substantial accumulated debt (approx. 43 trillion KRW loss between 2021-2023).
key_points: High and volatile industrial electricity rates relative to top global hubs.
Industrial users are targeted to cover KEPCO's financial deficits.
Direct Power Purchase (DPP) from the Korea Power Exchange is an option for large users to bypass KEPCO.

cost_model.name: Cost Model & Financial Projections
cost_model.content: Long-term cost projections are uncertain, with a high risk of continued sharp rate hikes (estimated at 3.5% CAGR) to offset KEPCO's debt and fund the 72.8 trillion KRW grid expansion. The high base rate and expected escalation result in a 20-year Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) projection that is significantly higher than competitor markets, impacting Total Cost of Ownership (TCO).
key_points: Significant risk of future cost hikes due to KEPCO's financial situation.
High projected LCOE makes the location less cost-competitive.
Market forecasts are driven by the need to fund massive infrastructure investment.

industrial_heritage.name: Industrial Heritage & Infrastructure
industrial_heritage.content: The location in Gyeonggi-do, a key part of the Greater Seoul tech and manufacturing corridor, benefits from an excellent industrial heritage. This includes proximity to existing high-voltage transmission corridors (345kV/765kV), a highly skilled electrical engineering and construction workforce, and established industrial zoning policies that can streamline development, despite the current power congestion.
key_points: Access to a dense network of existing HV transmission infrastructure.
Abundant availability of a highly skilled technical workforce.
Zoning and permitting are generally favorable for critical industrial infrastructure.

temperature_humidity.name: Temperature, Humidity & Free Cooling Potential
temperature_humidity.content: Anyang is characterized by a humid continental climate with hot, wet, and muggy summers, and cold, dry, freezing winters. The seasonal temperature swing is significant, which offers substantial opportunity for free cooling outside the summer months. The high humidity during the summer wet season (Changma) requires advanced dehumidification and cooling strategies.
key_points: Significant temperature swing (min -7C, max 30C) allows for estimated 5,000 free cooling hours/year, enabling PUE <1.3 potential.
High humidity during the wet season (July average 77%) necessitates robust dehumidification and careful management of ASHRAE A2 compliance.
Low winter temperatures simplify heating load management but require freeze protection for water-based cooling systems.

cooling_strategy.name: Flood Risk & Hydrological Hazards
cooling_strategy.content: CRITICAL: The site is located in an urban area (Anyang-si) away from the immediate coast, mitigating high-velocity coastal flood (V/VE) risk. Riverine flood risk is primarily associated with the Anyangcheon River basin. The Korean government provides Inundation Maps for flood-prone areas due to river overflow and insufficient urban drainage capacity.
key_points: NO-GO gate passed: Site is not coastal, therefore V/VE is not applicable. Assumed low-risk zone (equivalent to FEMA Zone X).
The primary flood hazard is riverine (Anyangcheon River) and urban flash flooding due to heavy rain and typhoons.
Site-specific engineering survey (HEC-RAS analysis equivalent) is required to confirm location outside the 100-year inundation map and assess urban drainage capacity.

free_cooling.name: Wildfire Risk & Vegetation Management
free_cooling.content: CRITICAL: Wildfire risk is significantly lower in the urbanized Gyeonggi-do area compared to the mountainous eastern regions (Gangwon-do). Recent severe wildfires have been concentrated in the east; the Gyeonggi area is assessed as a Low-Moderate risk due to urbanization.
key_points: NO-GO gate passed: Site is in an urban/industrial zone, assessed as low fire hazard risk.
Excellent fire department response time (estimated 3.0 km to nearest station) due to high urbanization.
Standard vegetation management (30m defensible space) is sufficient mitigation.

seismic_geological.name: Seismic Hazard & Geological Stability
seismic_geological.content: CRITICAL: The Korean Peninsula is generally a low-to-moderate seismic region. Probabilistic Seismic Hazard Analysis (PSHA) using instrumental and historical data suggests a low PGA value for the Gyeonggi area, well below the extreme NO-GO threshold. Active faults are poorly defined/non-existent near Anyang.
key_points: NO-GO gate passed: PGA is 0.10g, far below the 0.4g threshold for extreme hazard.
Moderate seismic design requirements (SDC C equivalent) add an estimated +15% structural cost for bracing and enhanced foundations.
Liquefaction risk is assigned as Moderate due to high precipitation and proximity to the Han River basin (necessitates geotechnical verification).

hydrological_flood.name: Protected Areas & Environmental Constraints
hydrological_flood.content: CRITICAL: Site is in a high-density urban/industrial area. Major WDPA Category I-III protected areas and UNESCO sites (natural) are distant. The risk of violating Riparian Buffer Zones (designation in Korea) or having on-site jurisdictional wetlands is low but requires verification.
key_points: NO-GO gate passed: No protected area violation expected within the urban/industrial zone.
Nearest major protected area (e.g., Bukhansan National Park) is estimated >10km away, providing a sufficient development buffer.
Low EIA complexity expected (estimated 6-9 months) unless site is adjacent to a Riparian Buffer Zone.

wind_storm.name: Wind, Storm & Tornado Risk
wind_storm.content: The Seoul Capital Area (including Anyang) is classified as a High cyclone/typhoon hazard zone, with an estimated >20% chance of damaging wind speeds (Typhoon/Very Strong Typhoon) in a 10-year period. Typhoons primarily bring high winds and intense rainfall (localized heavy rainfalls) leading to inland flooding. Tornado risk is low.
key_points: High wind hazard classification requires robust structural design (estimated +20% premium) to withstand Very Strong Typhoon-equivalent wind speeds.
Typhoon risk is dominated by wind and extreme rainfall (flash flooding), requiring heightened on-site drainage and roof-membrane integrity.
Structural design must account for the estimated 65 m/s design wind speed (based on 'High' hazard in Seoul area).

Increase in precipitation (10%) and heatwave days (15 days/year) indicates future stress on both drainage and cooling systems.
Inland location eliminates direct sea level rise risk, focusing resilience efforts on extreme heat and rainfall management.

competitive_landscape.name: Competitive Landscape Analysis
competitive_landscape.content: The Greater Seoul data center market is highly competitive and supply-constrained, with major global hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, GCP) and powerful domestic players (Naver Cloud, Kakao Enterprise, KT Cloud) vying for capacity. Total operational capacity in the Seoul Capital Area (SCA) is approximately 520 MW, with a massive 638 MW currently planned or under construction. Core market vacancy rates are critically low, dropping to approximately 6%, driving new development to proximate areas like Anyang/Gyeonggi-do and Incheon. The overall South Korean colocation market is forecasted to grow at an 18.6% CAGR to reach $7.228 billion by 2030.

peering_opportunities.name: Peering Opportunities & Network Ecosystem
peering_opportunities.content: Connectivity is excellent, anchored by Korea's status as one of the world's most connected nations. The market features four main IX operators: KT, SK Broadband, LG U+, and the sole carrier-neutral provider, KINX, which offers direct multi-cloud access (CloudHub) to all major hyperscalers. The region benefits from 4 cable landing stations across South Korea, which connect 11 cable segments, making Busan and the connected Seoul Capital Area a critical international gateway.

11 submarine cable landings ashore at four cable landing stations provide extensive international connectivity to Japan, Taiwan, and China.

infrastructure_scalability.name: Infrastructure Scalability & Future Growth
infrastructure_scalability.content: Infrastructure scalability in the SCA is severely constrained by power availability. Data center power demand is projected to reach 7,343 MW by 2027, exceeding the forecasted supply capacity of 4,718 MW, indicating an imminent power shortage and delays. Industrial electricity rates have recently risen by 9.7% for large businesses (to ~182.7 KRW/kWh or $0.13/kWh). Future growth is possible in proximate Gyeonggi-do (where this location lies) and through large-scale projects like the 1 GW AI center in Ulsan, but sites face mandatory Zero Energy Building (ZEB) requirements from 2025.

Industrial electricity rates have increased to ~182.7 KRW/kWh (approx. $0.13/kWh) for large businesses (Oct 2024), increasing operating costs.
New data center projects must comply with mandatory Zero Energy Building (ZEB) certification from 2025, adding complexity/cost to development.

executive_summary.location_overview: This location in the Gyeonggi-do cluster of the Seoul Metropolitan Area presents a compelling yet profoundly complex investment profile, characterized by world-class operational resilience countered by extreme execution friction and high operating costs; successful deployment is predicated on mitigating the 18-36 month power utility bottleneck and navigating severe social and regulatory resistance.
key_strengths: World-class utility resilience is guaranteed by KEPCOs highly reliable grid (4.7/5.0), combined with a low physical hazard profile (PGA 0.10g, Climate Analysis), providing a foundation for Tier IV uptime capabilities that minimizes operational expenditure related to unplanned outages.

Strategic market positioning is secured by unparalleled low latency access to over 50% of the South Korean demand concentration (Network Analysis) and a highly mature data protection framework (PIPA, EU Adequacy Decision), positioning the facility as a prime hub for compliant international hyperscale deployments.

Financial incentives exist through the regulatory environment, where investments focused on AI/HPC processing are eligible for substantial CapEx tax credits (15-25%), which directly offsets the high anticipated structural costs associated with typhoon hardening (+20% premium, Climate Analysis) and the complexity of local compliance architecture.

The sovereign credit rating of S&P AA and Moody's Aa2 (Risk Analysis) ensures a highly stable economic and political environment, mitigating macro-level financial uncertainty and providing confidence in long-term contract enforcement and stable governmental oversight.
key_challenges: The critical path is severely constrained by the trifecta of Power, Regulatory, and ESG friction: the 12-month minimum KEPCO confirmation timeline (Regulatory/Power) is compounded by the explicit government decentralization policy and the very high NIMBY risk (ESG), leading to an estimated 30-48 month time horizon before stable power delivery, significantly delaying Time-to-Market.

Long-term financial viability is threatened by the high and volatile industrial electricity rate (~$0.135/kWh) coupled with the necessity for expensive Carbon-Free Energy (CFE) procurement due to high grid carbon intensity (ESG ~425 gCO2/kWh), resulting in a high Levelized Cost of Electricity (LCOE) that reduces competitive advantage against lower-cost regional hubs.

Operational complexity arises from mandated data localization requirements for personal, financial, and location data (Risk Analysis), requiring significant upfront investment in sophisticated data segmentation architecture and potentially complex joint venture or corporate structuring to satisfy foreign investment screening mandates.

The structural design must accommodate extreme weather resilience (Climate Analysis), specifically requiring a +20% structural premium to withstand very strong typhoon winds and intense rainfall, demanding enhanced drainage and robust building envelopes beyond standard international designs.
critical_success_factors: Immediate and focused engagement with KEPCO and MOTIE is paramount to secure the power allocation slot, requiring a dedicated, high-level project management team to navigate the 12+ month confirmation bottleneck and demonstrate alignment with the government's energy efficiency regulations.

A mandatory, highly detailed, and proactive community engagement strategy (Social/ESG) must be implemented prior to submitting final permits to preemptively mitigate the very high NIMBY risk, potentially including community benefits agreements or localized infrastructure investment to ensure timeline stability.

Financial success is critically dependent upon securing a long-term, utility-scale Corporate PPA (Power/ESG) that provides stable, low-carbon energy pricing, thereby stabilizing the LCOE and insulating the project from KEPCO's highly volatile rate increases aimed at managing their substantial corporate debt.

The project scope must be meticulously defined to qualify for 'national strategic technology' status, ensuring the facility design maximizes eligibility for the 15-25% CapEx tax credits, which is essential for ROI given the high development and operational premiums in the SMA.

phase_1_deployment.recommended_capacity: The initial recommended deployment capacity is 50 Megawatts, strategically sized to secure the maximum feasible allocation without overwhelming immediate grid resources and minimizing initial CapEx exposure to the extended KEPCO timeline risk; scalability planning must ensure a clear pathway to 100 Megawatts coinciding with the planned post-2030 KEPCO infrastructure expansion completion.
phase_1_deployment.timeline: The comprehensive timeline for initial Phase 1 Ready-for-Service is projected at 42-48 months, extending beyond standard construction timelines due specifically to the critical interdependence of regulatory and power constraints; this includes 12 months for power confirmation, 6 months for pre-construction permitting (exacerbated by NIMBY risks), and a 24-30 month construction cycle incorporating enhanced structural resilience requirements.
priority_actions: Initiate immediate, high-priority engagement with KEPCO and MOTIE, securing the official Letter of Intent (LOI) for power capacity by prioritizing regulatory compliance efforts and demonstrating adherence to the Distributed Energy Act's requirements for distributed energy sourcing.

Finalize the cooling architecture and structural design immediately, incorporating the required +20% typhoon/wind structural premium (Climate Analysis) and implementing advanced dehumidification strategies to maximize the estimated 5,000 free cooling hours while ensuring ASHRAE A2 compliance during high summer humidity.

Establish the specific legal and data architecture framework tailored for handling localized data, satisfying both PIPA requirements and foreign investment screening mandates (Risk Analysis), ensuring client confidence in data sovereignty compliance before sales contracts are initiated.

Launch a comprehensive community and social impact mitigation program, assigning dedicated resources to proactive engagement to diffuse the very high NIMBY risk (ESG Analysis) and streamline the local permitting process by establishing transparent communication channels with local authorities.
phase_1_deployment.estimated_investment: Initial estimated investment for a 50MW Phase 1 deployment is projected at $450 Million to $550 Million, reflecting the significant premiums for land acquisition in Gyeonggi-do, the +20% structural hardening costs, the complex regulatory compliance architecture, and substantial CapEx allocated for necessary CFE PPA procurement to meet sustainability targets.
risk_mitigation: Mitigate the critical power timeline risk by establishing concurrent engineering pathways, commencing detailed design and material procurement for long-lead items (generators, switchgear) upon receipt of KEPCO's 6-month feasibility confirmation rather than waiting for the final 12-month power agreement, accelerating the construction phase.

Address the LCOE risk by negotiating a multi-year, dedicated Corporate Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) for clean energy to stabilize 50% of the operational load, using Direct Power Purchase (DPP) mechanisms to hedge against KEPCO's volatile rate hikes and simultaneously meet corporate ESG net-zero commitments.

Counter the geopolitical and localization risks by creating a compliant operational structure utilizing a subsidiary or joint venture focused exclusively on regulated Korean data (e.g., financial services), ring-fencing this high-risk data from general corporate workloads to maintain compliance and mitigate total revenue fine exposure.

Manage climate adaptation risk by designing the cooling infrastructure with a minimum +2.5C thermal margin (Climate Analysis), ensuring future-proofing against projected heatwave frequency and temperature increases, thereby protecting long-term operational resilience and PUE stability.

strategic_opportunities: The regulatory framework allows for strategic specialization, focusing the facility design and capacity deployment toward high-performance computing (HPC) and Artificial Intelligence workloads to fully leverage the 15-25% CapEx tax incentives, thereby financially mitigating the otherwise prohibitive operational and execution costs.

A strategic first-mover advantage can be achieved by aggressively pursuing the KEPCO interconnection slot, utilizing the massive, long-term 72.8 trillion KRW KEPCO grid investment plan to secure initial medium-scale capacity (e.g., 50MW) while retaining options for future 100MW+ scale expansion after the 2038 transmission upgrades are completed.

Establishing the facility as a compliant regional hub leverages the EU Adequacy Decision (Regulatory) and high reliability (Risk/Power), creating a premium service tier for multinational corporations requiring low latency to the Seoul market combined with stringent GDPR-equivalent data sovereignty guarantees.

The estimated 5,000 free cooling hours/year (Climate Analysis) presents an opportunity to implement advanced, hybrid cooling technologies that balance water usage with PUE optimization, strategically countering the high electricity cost base and improving overall sustainability metrics.
strategic_recommendation: The strategic recommendation is a CAUTIOUS GO, contingent upon the immediate execution of a highly disciplined, risk-mitigation strategy focused on accelerating the regulatory and power interconnection process while simultaneously maximizing available government incentives. This location represents irreplaceable market access and world-class resilience, justifying the high upfront cost and complex timeline, but the project must be treated as a regulatory and power execution challenge first, and a construction project second, prioritizing relationship management with KEPCO and mitigating high NIMBY risk through preemptive community negotiation.
conclusion: The final conclusion is a definitive GO with a Confidence Level of 75%, reflecting the high market opportunity offset by the significant and complex execution friction inherent in the Seoul Metropolitan Area. Success hinges entirely on two critical factors: First, securing and stabilizing the high operational cost structure via long-term CFE PPAs to counter KEPCOs high rates, and second, achieving power interconnection within the optimal 36-month timeline by proactively managing regulatory delays and aggressive NIMBY pushback. Failure to effectively manage the power/regulatory/social interface will result in critical project delays exceeding two years and significantly erode projected ROI.
next_steps: Establish the immediate project structure and allocate high-level resources to initiate the formal power application process with KEPCO, aiming to submit all necessary documentation for capacity impact assessment within 60 days.

Commission a detailed geotechnical survey and riverine flood analysis (equivalent to HEC-RAS) to finalize site engineering, specifically verifying the absence of liquefaction risk and confirming the location is outside the 100-year inundation map.

Formulate and budget the detailed ESG community engagement plan immediately, preparing the required negotiation and compensation packages necessary to proactively address and neutralize anticipated NIMBY resistance during the local permitting phase.

assumptions_made.assumption: Exchange Rate: 1 USD = 1350 KRW for cost conversions.
SAIDI/SAIFI figures are estimated based on KEPCO's historical trend of world-class performance and targets.
Demand Charge is estimated at $15.0/kW-month based on market data for similar high-cost industrial regions in Asia.
Available capacity is an estimate of residual capacity at the nearest major substation before requiring trunk-line extension.
LCOE is a simplified 20-year projection based on the $0.135/kWh base rate and 3.5% annual escalation.
Analysis uses Anyang, Gyeonggi-do, South Korea for regional hazard data.
FEMA/CAL FIRE/USGS standards are proxied using South Korean official data (e.g., Inundation Maps, KFS Landslide Maps) and international models (GEM).
Flood risk (FEMA Zone X equivalent) is assumed due to urban location away from Anyangcheon's main inundation area  requires site-specific inundation map review.
PGA of 0.10g is a conservative estimate for the Gyeonggi area PSHA (475-year return) based on GEM and Korean studies.
Climate change projections (2050) are based on a conservative RCP8.5 or equivalent high-emissions pathway proxy (e.g., 2.5C warming by 2050).
Political Stability Index (0-10) is a linear conversion of the World Bank WGI (-2.5 to 2.5) score of 0.61.
Crime Rate is based on the 2014 national total crime-per-100k as a conservative proxy for the dense urban Gyeonggi-do area.
KEPCO SAIDI is estimated at 80 min/year based on historical data indicating a world-class, continuously improving grid, which places it in the 'Excellent' category.
Emergency response times and distances are estimated based on Gyeonggi-do's high urban density and known municipal service levels, targeting NFPA 1710 standards.

WRI Aqueduct Water Stress for the Seoul Metropolitan Area is classified as Medium-High/High (Score 2-4) due to high population and industrial density, leading to greater competition for water resources.
The baseline grid carbon intensity is conservatively estimated at ~425 gCO/kWh, a mid-point of reported 2021/2022 figures (411.3 - 436 gCO/kWh).
Standard international certifications (e.g., LEED, BREEAM) and ISO management systems are readily available and recognized in the market.
The 50-100MW project falls under the strict environmental and power-related regulations (e.g., >10MW power assessment and SMA Distributed Energy requirements).
The site is within the constrained Seoul Metropolitan Area (SMA)/Gyeonggi-do, subjecting it to decentralization policy pressure.
Hyperscaler analysis is based on publicly announced regions (AWS Seoul, Azure Korea Central/South, GCP Seoul) and known expansion patterns within the Seoul Capital Area (SCA).
Quantitative metrics for the specific coordinates are extrapolated from Seoul/SCA market data, as the location (Anyang/Gyeonggi-do) falls within this primary data center cluster.
Pricing and capacity metrics are approximations based on market reports and may not reflect specific wholesale Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) negotiations.

all_no_go_gates.reason: Site is inland (Anyang) and non-coastal, thus V/VE (high-velocity coastal flood zone) is not applicable.
all_no_go_gates.standard_reference: FEMA regulations prohibit cost-effective data center construction in V/VE zones

all_no_go_gates.reason: Site is assumed to be outside the primary flood hazard area, making BFE negligible or non-existent (Zone X equivalent).
all_no_go_gates.standard_reference: Building codes require FFE = BFE + 0.6m; sites with BFE >3m face prohibitive costs

all_no_go_gates.reason: Site is in an urban/industrial area of Gyeonggi-do, assessed as low fire hazard risk.
all_no_go_gates.standard_reference: CAL FIRE Very High FHSZ has >30% fire impact probability per decade

all_no_go_gates.reason: PSHA for the Gyeonggi area is low-moderate, estimated PGA 0.10g, below the 0.4g threshold.
all_no_go_gates.standard_reference: ASCE 7 Seismic Design Category E/F (PGA >0.4g) triggers prohibitive structural costs
all_no_go_gates.mitigation_cost: Not applicable - NO-GO gate passed (would be $80-150M for seismic isolation if triggered)

all_no_go_gates.reason: No WDPA Category I-III protected areas or UNESCO buffer zones are expected within a 10km radius of this urban/industrial site.
all_no_go_gates.standard_reference: IUCN protected area categories I-III prohibit large-scale industrial development

all_no_go_gates.reason: The EU-Korea Adequacy Decision (GDPR Article 45) and PIPA's consent/contract mechanisms permit lawful international data flows.

all_caution_flags.cost_impact: +$5M for delayed project financing, specialist consultants (power/environmental)

all_caution_flags.description: The combined regulatory load (12+ month power bottleneck, decentralization policy, resident opposition risk in SMA) leads to a likely 18-24 month pre-construction approval timeline, and a 3-4 year total development cycle.

all_caution_flags.cost_impact: +$10M for extended legal/consulting and carrying costs
